snippet.title: Vincenzo Peruggia: The Man Who Stole The Mona Lisa
snippet.description:
In 1911, the world was rocked by the "unimaginable" news: the Mona Lisa had been stolen from the Louvre. For over two years, the masterpiece was truly gone, leaving the "greatest detectives in the world" clueless and leading to the interrogation of famous figures like Pablo Picasso. In this documentary, we retrace the footsteps of Vincenzo Peruggia, the house painter who walked out of the museum with Da Vinci’s treasure wrapped in his smock. Through exclusive interviews with Peruggia’s 84-year-old daughter, Celestina, and access to long-lost psychiatric reports and personal letters, we strip away the myths.

snippet.title: What Medieval Kyiv Looked Like 1,000 Years Ago Before History Forgot It (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, I use AI to "resurrect" Kyiv — the Viking capital of the Slavic world — and walk its streets exactly as they were around 1050 AD, right before the empire it built began to fracture from within. It's not just about looking at buildings; we explore the massive slave-trading docks of the Podol, the golden domes of Saint Sophia rising above the Dnieper, and the ceremonial Golden Gate at the absolute peak of their power. We contrast that extraordinary reality — where a Slavic-Viking-Byzantine hybrid ruled more territory than the Holy Roman Empire — with the fragments and ruins that survive today.

We also break down the exact moment a young warlord returned from exile, drowned his own pagan gods in a river, and built a Christian empire in a single generation. It's crazy to see what was actually lost to history, especially since a Kievan princess signed her name in Cyrillic on a French throne — decades before the Normans ever crossed the Channel.

snippet.title: How Bike Brakes Upgraded Over The Years 😳
snippet.description: Bike brakes used to be dangerously unreliable but here’s how they got fixed!Back in the 1800s the stopping mechanism was ridiculously simple, where a rubber chunk was pushed against the spinning wheel. But this crumbled fast and only sometimes worked during rainfall. But things changed completely in the 1950s where the pads grabbed the metal circle running around the wheel. This made their braking ability so much better, way more powerful, consistent and this is design has not changed because its how all bike brakes work now!

snippet.title: Knossos 1700 BC: Europe's First Civilization (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
In this video! I’m taking you straight back to the island of Crete in the year 1700 BC, where Europe’s very first civilization is reaching its absolute peak.

I’ve used AI to reconstruct the legendary Palace of Knossos. You’ll see a massive complex of over 1,000 rooms with no fortification walls , featuring a plumbing system with flushing toilets that wouldn't be matched in Europe for another 3,000 years.


But the most intense part is seeing how this society was completely different from anything else in history. I explain how this was a civilization ruled not by kings, but by high priestesses , and how they faced two apocalyptic catastrophes: a volcanic explosion with the force of millions of atomic bombs , followed by an invasion of warriors from mainland Greece.


It’s crazy to see how this peaceful, goddess-worshiping culture was transformed into the myths of the Labyrinth and the Minotaur. Check it out and let me know which lost civilization I should reconstruct next!

snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Apprentice (Black Death) | day 1 of 7
snippet.description:
It is November 1348. London has 80,000 people. The plague arrived three weeks ago.

Nobody is talking about it. Not openly. Not yet.

This is Day 1 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are a 16-year-old apprentice on Cheapside — the loudest, busiest, most extraordinary street in medieval England. You sleep on a straw pallet on your master's workshop floor. You eat dark gritty bread and small ale for breakfast. You carry bolts of broadcloth through streets named after the things they sell — Bread Street, Milk Street, Honey Lane, Goldsmiths Row.

And this morning, on an errand near St Mary-le-Bow, you see something in a churchyard that you cannot stop thinking about.

The swellings have started. The bells are ringing more than usual. Your master burns rosemary in the doorway and tells you not to linger in crowds. The city is going about its ordinary business. And somewhere underneath the noise of Cheapside, something is very wrong.

Using AI trained on medieval chronicles, guild records, and archaeological evidence, we've reconstructed what one ordinary day in London looked like in the last week before everything changed.

Day 1 — The Apprentice (you are here)

snippet.title: What 1700s New York Really Looked Like (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
What if you could walk the streets of Manhattan before the skyscrapers, the neon lights, and the grid? In this immersive documentary, we use cutting-edge AI reconstruction to resurrect New York City in the 1700s. By bridging the gap between 18th-century archaeology and advanced generative technology, we bring history to life in high definition—revealing a city built on ambition, grit, and rebellion.

18th-century New York was never just a quiet colonial town; it was a rough-edged outpost of 20,000 people pulsing with the energy of global maritime trade. From the political conspiracies whispered in Fraunces Tavern to the strategic cannons guarding The Battery, we explore how the city’s early foundations were forged in the shadow of the British Empire.

Witness the "Architecture of Ambition" as we investigate the opulent wealth of the Morris-Jumel Mansion, the environmental tragedy of Collect Pond, and the daily struggle for survival in the cramped wooden tenements of Lower Manhattan. Using AI-driven visuals, we peel back the layers of time to show you the colonial reality that the history books often miss.

In this video, you will experience:

Digital Resurrection: See Wall Street and St. Paul’s Chapel exactly as they appeared in 1776.

The Strategic Harbor: How Fort George protected the city's maritime lifeblood.

The Price of Freedom: The bloody legacy of the Old Stone House and the Battle of Brooklyn.

The Social Internet: How 18th-century markets served as the city's pulse and "melting pot."

Daily Struggles: The raw, human reality of living in a pre-industrial metropolis.

Why use AI for History?
History is often trapped in dusty maps and fading fragments. By utilizing AI reconstruction, we can experience the true scale, shadows, and sensory reality of a civilization that laid the groundwork for the modern world. This is New York history, reimagined for the digital age.

snippet.title: Pre Historic Megastructure On The Mountains Of Bolivia
snippet.description: Join us as we explore the high-altitude mysteries of Tiwanaku and Puma Punku, home to prehistoric megastructures perched over 12,000 feet above sea level in the Andes Mountains of Bolivia. This journey into the heart of an ancient empire reveals a level of stone masonry that seems almost impossible for the era, featuring massive andesite blocks weighing over 130 tons that were transported across rugged terrain without the use of modern machinery. First, we examine the "H-blocks" of Puma Punku, which exhibit such perfect right angles and smooth surfaces that they resemble modern modular construction or precision machine-cutting. Second, we dive into the sophisticated irrigation and drainage systems that once supported a thriving urban population in this harsh, thin-air environment. Third, we investigate the Gate of the Sun, a monolithic archway carved from a single block of stone, adorned with intricate astronomical and religious iconography that hints at a deep understanding of the cosmos. Fourth, we look at the Akapana Pyramid, a massive terraced structure that was once clad in gleaming blue stone and served as the spiritual center of this megalithic complex. Fifth, we explore the mystery of how these ancient builders achieved such tight tolerances—where even a razor blade cannot fit between stones—using only primitive tools. Finally, we reflect on the sudden decline of this civilization and the haunting ruins they left behind, which continue to challenge our timeline of human technological development and architectural history.

snippet.title: What Did New York Look Like in 1650? (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
What did New York City look like in 1650 — before the skyscrapers, before the grid, before any of it?
Most people have never seen it. Not really.
Using advanced AI reconstruction built on historical maps, colonial records, and archaeological research, we travel back to a time when Manhattan was still a small Dutch outpost called New Amsterdam — a muddy, windswept trading post at the edge of the known world, clinging to the southern tip of an island most Europeans had never heard of.
No skyscrapers. No subway. No crowds.
Just dirt paths through marshland, wooden houses facing the harbor, a half-built fort, a single canal, and about 1,000 people trying to make a life at the bottom of an island that would one day hold 8 million.
This video brings that world back to life — not as paintings, not as old maps — but as a fully immersive, cinematic reconstruction of what New Amsterdam may have actually looked and felt like nearly 400 years ago.

New Amsterdam in 1650 — the real layout, streets, and skyline
Daily life inside one of the first European settlements in North America
The original landscape of Manhattan before it was reshaped
The Dutch trading culture that quietly laid the foundations of New York City
How a tiny colonial outpost became one of the most powerful cities in history

snippet.title: Life 4,600 Years Ago | How Early Humans Built The Pyramid
snippet.description: Join us as we explore the incredible engineering, social organization, and daily grit required to construct the Great Pyramid of Giza over 4,600 years ago. This journey takes you back to the Old Kingdom of Egypt, where we dismantle the myth of slave labor and reveal a highly organized workforce of skilled laborers who were housed, fed, and respected for their monumental contributions. First, we examine the sophisticated quarrying techniques used to extract millions of limestone and granite blocks using only copper tools and wooden wedges. Second, we dive into the mathematical precision of the pyramid’s alignment, which remains nearly perfect to the true north, a feat achieved through advanced astronomical observations. Third, we investigate the likely ramp systems and water-lubricated sledges used to transport stones weighing several tons across the desert sands. Fourth, we look at the logistics of the "Pyramid City," a massive support hub that provided medical care and rations for thousands of workers and their families. Fifth, we explore the spiritual motivation behind these structures, which served as "resurrection machines" to ensure the Pharaoh's eternal journey among the stars. Finally, we reflect on how these ancient builders managed to create the tallest man-made structure on Earth for over 3,800 years, leaving behind a legacy that continues to challenge our understanding of human capability and ancient technology

snippet.title: Medieval London 1348 | A Day in the Life of an Grave Digger (Black Death) | day 4 of 7
snippet.description:
When archaeologists excavated East Smithfield in London in 1986, they found something unexpected.

The bodies weren't buried randomly. They were laid out in neat rows — perfectly aligned, hands folded, shrouded where possible. Over ten thousand of them. In less than two years.

Somebody did that work. Thousands of times. In November mud. For very little pay. And nobody ever wrote their name down.

This is Day 4 of our 7-part series: A Week in Medieval London.

Today, you are a gravedigger at East Smithfield — the emergency burial ground the Bishop of London consecrated in November 1348 because the parish churchyards were already full. You sleep in a lean-to shelter at the edge of the site. You eat dark bread before dawn. You dig trenches alongside a man named Walter who has made a private agreement with himself about what this job is and is not, and who has not shared the terms of that agreement with anyone.

The carts come every morning. You lay the bodies in rows, east to west, the way the Christian tradition requires — so that when they rise at the Last Judgement they will face Jerusalem. You fold their hands where folding is possible. You do this thirty times today.

One of them is a child wrapped in a blue wool blanket with an embroidered flower near the corner. Someone sewed that flower on an ordinary day that was not this day.

You notice it. You don't mention it to Walter. You go back to the digging.

Using AI trained on the Museum of London's excavation reports and medieval city records, we've reconstructed what one day as a gravedigger at East Smithfield actually looked like in November 1348.

Day 4 — The Gravedigger (you are here)

snippet.title: Life 7 Million Years Ago | Survival of the Last Woman of the Savannah
snippet.description:
Life 7 Million Years Ago | Survival of the Last Woman of the Savannah
Step back into a world untouched by time — a world of ancient predators, harsh landscapes, and the struggle to survive. This documentary-style story follows the last woman of the savannah, living in a prehistoric world 7 million years ago, where every day is a battle against nature, hunger, and danger.

From escaping saber-tooth beasts to building shelters, finding food, studying predators, and learning the rules of the wild, this film shows how early humans adapted and fought for survival. Experience the savannah as it once was — filled with giant snakes, ancient elephants, fierce hunters, and the constant threat of extinction.

This video explores:
• Prehistoric savannah life
• Early human survival skills
• Predator vs. prey behavior
• Primitive tools and shelters
• Realistic reconstruction of life millions of years ago

Immerse yourself in a dramatic, emotional, and visually detailed journey of the last surviving woman in a world before civilization.

No animal or human being was harmed during the creation of this story.

If you enjoy prehistoric stories, survival documentaries, and ancient world explorations, this is for you.
